This chart is redrawn from a mining company's annual report. What is misleading about it, and how would you fix it?

The 1970 net income was a loss of $11,014, yet its bar points up like a profit. The bars also do not start at zero, so a tiny value like $75,243 looks almost as tall as $351,341, and the tallest bars in all three panels are the same height even though $7.4 million is far more than $1.2 million. Fix: draw every bar from a zero baseline on one common axis, with the 1970 loss going below zero.

The loss in 1970 is shown as a positive bar going up. Heights are not proportional to the numbers since there is no zero baseline. I would add a y-axis starting at 0 and draw the loss as a negative bar under the zero line.

Net income in 1970 was negative but it is drawn upward like a gain. Each panel uses its own scale, so 1.2 million and 7.4 million look the same height. Put all three panels on one common scale that starts at zero and let the loss bar drop below zero.
The 1970 net income bar is the problem: it was a loss, but the bar goes up like it was a profit.

Describe this chart in grammar-of-graphics terms: the aesthetic mappings, the geom, and one more layer.

Data: Miami's 2026 games, one row per game. Aesthetics: x = point differential (Miami minus opponent), y = opponent, fill = site (home or away). Geom: geom_col bars. One more layer: facet_grid that splits non-conference and MAC games.
ggplot(games, aes(x = margin, y = opponent, fill = site)) + geom_col() + geom_vline(xintercept = 0) + facet_grid(conference ~ .)

Each bar is one game and its length is how many points Miami won or lost by; the opponent is on the y axis and the color is home vs away. The geom is bars. There is also a facet layer that separates the MAC games from the non-conference games.
It is a bar chart, so the geom is geom_col.
The chart is split into two facets, one panel for non-conference games and one for MAC games.
x = opponent, y = margin, fill = result (red means Miami won), drawn with geom_col.
